slides.title: Application Grammar
slides.notes: Open the lecture by stressing that Chapter 12 is not a new algebraic universe; it is the homogeneous model being used as a programming language for incidence, projection, camera geometry, and diagnostics. The title slide previews the recurring pattern: choose representatives, apply a linear map or product, then test an invariant.

slides.title: Join And Meet Grammar
slides.notes: Use this slide to fix the grammar. A join builds the smallest projective object containing the given ingredients, while a meet recovers their common part. Keep the language concrete: two points generate a line, two planes meet in a line, and every later camera construction is just this grammar with matrices attached.

slides.title: Plucker Lines
slides.notes: Explain Plucker coordinates as the line blade seen through an implementation lens. The direction tells how the line points, and the moment tells how it misses the origin. The two checks on the slide are small but decisive: shifting along the line preserves the moment, and d dot m remains zero.

slides.title: Incidence As Tests
slides.notes: Incidence is where the algebra starts paying rent. Rather than branching over many special cases, the code asks whether a line direction is tangent to the plane and whether one point on the line satisfies the plane equation. The blade statement and the dot-product statement are two interfaces to the same test.

slides.title: Line Pair Taxonomy
slides.notes: Frame the four line relationships as outputs of one representation rather than separate recipes. Intersecting and coincident lines are exact incidence cases, parallel lines expose a degenerate direction bivector, and skew lines produce a shortest connector. The connector being orthogonal to both directions is the computational certificate.

slides.title: Projective Transform Adapter
slides.notes: Describe a homogeneous matrix as an adapter between algebra and graphics APIs. Points move by direct multiplication, planes move by inverse transpose, and lines may be rebuilt from transformed endpoints. The practical invariant is simple: incidence before the transform must still be incidence after the transform.

slides.title: Vanishing Points
slides.notes: Vanishing points are a good sanity check for projective thinking because nothing mystical happens at infinity. A family of parallel world lines shares an ideal direction; the camera maps that direction to a finite image point when it is not parallel to the image plane. The diagram asks students to see the point as an image of a direction.

slides.title: Pinhole Projection
slides.notes: Emphasize that the image coordinate is only a representative of a ray. Scaling the homogeneous image vector does not change the observation, and dividing by the last coordinate is a display step. The projection matrix, its null-space camera center, and the back-projected ray are the same data organized three ways.

slides.title: Epipolar Incidence
slides.notes: Use the epipolar slide to replace search intuition with incidence. A point in the left image chooses a ray, the right camera center joins that ray into a plane, and the right image sees a line. The displayed near-zero residual comes from the notebook check and confirms the exact synthetic correspondences.

slides.title: Line-Based Stereo
slides.notes: Line-based stereo is the dual version of point stereo. An observed image line back-projects to a whole plane of rays, so two views recover a spatial line by meeting planes. The alignment and endpoint residuals give students a numerical target: the recovered line is not just drawn, it is certified.

slides.title: Interpolation With Representatives
slides.notes: Interpolation is included to keep the lecture honest about animation and calibration workflows. Homogeneous representatives can be blended only after a convention is chosen and must be normalized before interpretation. For rigid or camera transforms, interpolate meaningful parameters or a group logarithm, then recheck incidence instead of trusting the picture.

slides.title: Computational Check Board
slides.notes: Close with the check board, not a generic summary. Each application has a measurable invariant: Plucker orthogonality, epipolar residuals, ray-plane containment, reconstruction error, view-matrix convention, and skew-line perpendicularity. The final message is that homogeneous modeling is useful because it gives both constructions and tests.
